subject: maths

concepts.title: Natural Numbers
concepts.definition: The numbers 1, 2, 3, ... arose when early herders tracked cattle with pebbles, pairing each animal with one marker; the same idea appears as tally notches cut into ancient bone. Taking a smaller number away from a bigger one is impossible inside this set, which is what pushed the subject forward.
concepts.key_idea: Start at one; every element is a whole unit; subtraction can fall out of the set.
question_patterns: What do we count with, in the set 1, 2, 3, ...?
Are the natural numbers closed under subtraction? Give a reason.
Explain how herders paired cattle with pebbles to keep count.
Name the set that grew out of tally marks and one-to-one pairing.
Why did tracing trade and astronomy push people beyond 1, 2, 3, ...?

solution_steps.explain: A member must be a whole number starting from 1 with nothing after the point.
If the subtraction dips below 1, the result leaves the set.
Natural numbers are closed under addition and multiplication but not under subtraction, since results like 3 - 5 fall outside the set.

concepts.title: Multiplying by Zero: Brahmagupta's Rule
concepts.definition: In his 628 CE work, Brahmagupta equipped the void with full arithmetic: add it or take it away and every number stays as it was, but a product with it always collapses to nothing.
concepts.key_idea: a + 0 and a - 0 preserve a; a x 0 wipes the board.
question_patterns: What is 8 x 0?
Find the product of 125 and 0.
State the value of (-15) x 0.
Explain why a x 0 = 0 for every number a.
Complete the product: (-7) x 0 = ?

solution_steps.explain: Any number times zero is zero.
Confirm that a + 0 = a and a - 0 = a, so zero preserves every number under addition and subtraction.
The product collapses to zero regardless of the sign or size of the other factor.

concepts.title: Arithmetic of Integers
concepts.definition: Brahmagupta read signs through trade: wealth (dhana) counts as plus and debt (rina) counts as minus. His sign laws still decide every product: two like signs give wealth, two unlike signs give debt.
concepts.formula: product sign: like signs give plus, unlike signs give minus
concepts.key_idea: Like signs pair into plus; unlike signs fall to minus.
concepts.textbook_ref: iemh103.txt lines 149-202 (section 3.3, rules 1-5, Think and Reflect)
question_patterns: Find the product (-8) x (-7).
Calculate (-12) x 5.
Multiply (-20) by 4.
A trader takes 4 debts of 3 rupees each; what is the total as a signed number?
Work out the sign and the value of (-6) x (+9).

solution_steps.action: Multiply the sizes, then attach the sign
solution_steps.explain: Two debts give a fortune; a debt with a fortune gives a debt.

solution_steps.action: Determine the sign from the pair
solution_steps.explain: Like signs (both positive or both negative) yield a positive product; unlike signs yield a negative product.

solution_steps.action: Combine magnitude and sign for the answer
solution_steps.explain: The absolute values give the size and the sign rule gives the direction, producing the final signed product.

concepts.title: Definition of Rational Numbers
concepts.definition: Rational status belongs to a value whenever some fraction with integer top and non-zero bottom, fully reduced, lands exactly on it; every integer qualifies with bottom 1.
concepts.formula: rational = p / q with integer p, integer q and q not zero
concepts.key_idea: If it folds into a ratio of two whole values, it belongs; bottoms never hit zero.
question_patterns: What makes a number rational?
Is -7 a rational number? Justify your answer.
Decide whether 0 is rational and explain why.
Show that 4/6 and 2/3 name one and the same rational number.
Which single number has every integer as its top with bottom 1?

solution_steps.explain: Seek integer top p and non-zero integer bottom q with p/q equal to the number.
If such a pair exists in fully reduced form, the number is rational.
The denominator q must never be zero, since division by zero is undefined; this is the one hard requirement for rational status.

concepts.title: Multiplying Rational Numbers
concepts.definition: To multiply two fractions, multiply the tops together for the new top and the bottoms together for the new bottom, then reduce the result.
concepts.key_idea: Tops with tops, bottoms with bottoms, then simplify.
question_patterns: Find the product 2/3 x 3/10.
Multiply 7/11 by 5/8.
Calculate (-4/7) x 5/14.
What is 5/4 x 2/3? Reduce your answer.
Work out the product of 9/2 and 2/9.

solution_steps.explain: Top of the first times top of the second.
Bottom of the first times bottom of the second.
The product value is top over bottom.

concepts.title: Adding Rational Numbers
concepts.definition: To add (or subtract) fractions, give them a common bottom by cross-multiplying, combine the tops, then reduce; subtraction flips the second top's sign first.
concepts.key_idea: Match the bottoms, add the tops, reduce the result.
question_patterns: Find the sum 2/5 + 3/10.
Add 7/12 and 5/8.
Calculate (-4/7) + 3/14.

solution_steps.explain: Each top is scaled by the other fraction's bottom.
Second top times first bottom.
Their sum rides over the common bottom.
Product of the two bottoms.
The combined value is top over bottom.

concepts.title: Density of Rational Numbers
concepts.definition: No matter how tightly two fractions squeeze together, one more always slips in between: halve their sum and repeat. Such numbers leave no breathing room on the line.
concepts.key_idea: The mean lands strictly inside; repeat forever.
question_patterns: Find a rational number strictly between -1/2 and 1/4.
How many rationals lie between 3.1415 and 3.1416?
Insert two fractions between 1 and 2 by repeated averaging.
Explain why the mean of two rationals stays rational.
Name a fraction that sits between 5/4 and 3/2.

solution_steps.explain: Sum the given pair.
The average is a rational strictly between them.
The average of two distinct rationals is itself rational and falls strictly inside the interval, so the process can be repeated to insert infinitely many rationals.

concepts.title: Representing Rationals on the Number Line
concepts.definition: To place a fraction p/q, cut each whole step into q equal pieces, then step p pieces right for positives and left for negatives; improper fractions land past 1 after carrying the wholes.
concepts.formula: denominator cuts, numerator steps, sign picks the side
concepts.key_idea: Cut by the bottom, step by the top, carry wholes for tops past the bottom.
question_patterns: Show 3/4 on a number line.
Where does -3/4 sit relative to -1 and 0?
Locate 9/4: between which two integers does it fall, and how is the interval cut?
Draw a line and place 2/3, -5/4 and 11/2 in order.
Explain why 1/2 sits exactly halfway between 0 and 1.

solution_steps.explain: Divide each whole step into q equal pieces.
Move p pieces from 0, right for positive p and left for negative p; carry wholes first for improper tops.
The landing point on the line is the rational number p/q, confirming the fraction has a unique position on the number line.

concepts.title: Distance Between Two Rationals
concepts.definition: The two-sided bars around a difference answer one question: how far apart? Sign is discarded, so the gap between points a and b is the same bars around a - b, and it never comes out negative.
concepts.key_idea: Bars measure, never judge: the gap is unsigned.
question_patterns: How far apart are -4 and 3 on a number line?
Find the distance between 2 and -7.
What is |a - b| for a = -1 and b = 5?
Calculate the gap between 3/4 and 1/4 on a line.
Two towns sit at marks -8 and 6 on a map line; find the separation.

solution_steps.explain: Form the difference of the two positions.
The bars make the gap unsigned.

solution_steps.action: Interpret the result as a length
solution_steps.explain: The non-negative value is the number of unit steps between the two points on the line, independent of order.

concepts.title: Irrational Numbers
concepts.definition: Some lengths, like a square's diagonal over its side, refuse every fraction: their decimal tails run on endlessly, never settling into any looping cycle. Hippasus proved this for the unit square's diagonal by trapping a coprime fraction in an impossible position.
concepts.formula: diagonal of unit square = sqrt(2), which has no fraction form
concepts.key_idea: Not every length folds into a fraction; the unit square's diagonal was the first shock.
question_patterns: Prove that the diagonal of a unit square is irrational.
Walk through Hippasus's contradiction for the square root of 2.
Classify sqrt(81), sqrt(12) and 0.333... as rational or irrational.
Why can no fraction equal pi exactly?
State the one property that makes a number irrational.

solution_steps.explain: Suppose root 2 equals p/q with coprime integers p and q.
p squared equals 2 q squared, so p must be even; write p = 2k.
q squared equals 2 k squared, so q is even too.
Both even contradicts coprimality, so no such fraction exists.

concepts.title: Constructing Square-Root Lengths
concepts.definition: A ruler-and-compass recipe lands irrational measures on the line: raise a right-angle unit leg at the unit mark, join its tip to the origin to form the diagonal, then swing that diagonal down onto the line with an arc.
concepts.formula: OA = 1, AB = 1 gives OB = sqrt(2); arcs copy lengths
concepts.key_idea: Right-angle unit legs make a sqrt(2) diagonal; arcs copy it onto the line.
question_patterns: Construct a segment of length sqrt(2) and mark it on a line.
Explain the three steps for placing sqrt(2) on a number line.
How would you extend the method to sqrt(3)?
Why does the joined segment OB have length sqrt(2)?
Sketch the construction needed for sqrt(5).

solution_steps.explain: At the unit mark A, draw a perpendicular and mark B one unit up.
OB is the diagonal of a unit square, hence sqrt(2).
Centre O, radius OB: the arc cuts the line at the new irrational length.

concepts.title: The Story of Pi
concepts.definition: Pi pairs a circle's girth with its width and never settles into a fraction. Aryabhata offered 3.1416 while labelling it an asanna, a near-value; Madhava went further, with an endless alternating sum of odd reciprocals, times 4, closing in on pi.
concepts.key_idea: One stubborn irrational, two responses: better near-values, or an exact infinite sum.
question_patterns: Whose infinite series first expressed pi exactly?
Approximate pi using the first three terms of Madhava's series.
Why can no fraction equal pi exactly?
What did Aryabhata mean by calling 3.1416 an asanna?
Write the first four terms of the odd-reciprocal series for pi.

solution_steps.explain: Summing 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ... and scaling by 4 approaches pi.
Each extra term tightens the approximation; no finite stop lands exactly on pi.
Since no fraction equals pi and the series never terminates, pi is irrational; every finite sum is only an asanna, a near-value.

concepts.title: Predicting Decimal Expansion Type
concepts.definition: Reduce fully first, then split the bottom into primes: bottoms built purely from 2s and 5s stop the division dead; any other prime sends the digits into an endless loop.
concepts.formula: stop condition: bottom's primes are 2s and 5s only
concepts.key_idea: Bottom primes of 2 and 5 mean a stopping decimal; anything else loops.
question_patterns: Will 7/20 stop or loop as a decimal? Reason without dividing.
Decide the decimal fate of 4/15 and 13/250.
What property of the bottom decides termination?
Sort 3/50, 2/9 and 7/8 into stopping and looping.
Why does 1/7 loop forever?

solution_steps.explain: Cancel common factors so top and bottom share nothing.
Only 2s and 5s: the decimal stops. Any other prime: the digits loop.
A stopping bottom means a terminating decimal; any other prime factor means a non-terminating repeating decimal, with no other outcome possible.

concepts.title: Terminating Decimals to Fractions
concepts.definition: Count the places after the point, put the digits over 1 followed by that many zeros, then reduce: 0.35 lands as 35 over 100, which shrinks to 7/20.
concepts.formula: places after the point become zeros downstairs
concepts.key_idea: Places become zeros downstairs; cancel everything common.
question_patterns: Convert 0.35 into p/q form.
Write 12.6 as a fraction in lowest terms.
Express 3.05 as a ratio of integers.
Turn 0.0120 into a fully reduced fraction.
Which power of ten goes downstairs for 2.05?

solution_steps.explain: The count sets the power of ten downstairs.
Digits without the point go on top; 1 followed by that many zeros goes below.
Cancel common factors, e.g. 35/100 down to 7/20.

concepts.title: Pure Repeating Decimals to Fractions
concepts.definition: When a fixed digit block cycles from the point onward, shift one full cycle with a power of ten, subtract the original, and the endless tail cancels: 0.666... becomes 6 over 9, or 2/3.
concepts.formula: one nine downstairs per looping digit
concepts.key_idea: One nine downstairs per looping digit; the loop dissolves.
question_patterns: Convert 0.6 with the 6 repeating into p/q form.
Express 0.454545... as a fraction.
Show that 0.45 with both digits repeating equals 5/11.
How many nines go downstairs for a 3-digit repeating block?
Turn 0.142857 with the block repeating into a fraction.

solution_steps.explain: Write x = 0.666... for example.
One repeating digit: multiply by 10; two: by 100, and so on.
The shifted read minus x kills the infinite tail; solve for x and reduce.

concepts.title: General Repeating Decimals to Fractions
concepts.definition: Mixed cases need two shifts: first push the plain digits past the point, then push one full cycle, and subtract the two shifted reads; 2.357 with only the 7 repeating reduces to 1061/450.
concepts.key_idea: Shift to purify, shift one cycle, subtract: the leftover bottom mixes 9s and 0s.
question_patterns: Convert 2.357 with only the 7 repeating into p/q form.
Express 0.16 with the 6 repeating as a fraction.
Which shift clears the non-repeating digits first?
Turn 1.235 with 35 repeating into a fraction in lowest terms.
Why do zeros appear among the nines in the denominator?

solution_steps.explain: Multiply by 10 once per non-repeating digit.
Multiply once more by 10 per repeating digit.
Subtract the first shifted equation from the second; solve and reduce.

concepts.title: Cyclic Numbers
concepts.definition: Divide 1 by 7 and the block 142857 repeats forever - and it multiplies like a carousel: times 1 through 6 merely spins the same six digits. Such rotating blocks are known as cyclic.
concepts.key_idea: One-seventh's block rotates in place when scaled by 1 through 6.
question_patterns: What makes 142857 a cyclic number?
Which fraction produces the repeating block 142857?
Compute 142857 x 5 and describe the result.
Multiply the block by 3 and check the circular shift of digits.
Find the repeating block of 1/13 by long division.

solution_steps.explain: 1 divided by 7 gives the repeating block 142857.
Products with 1 through 6 cycle the same digits in a circle.
If every multiplier from 1 to one-less-than-the-block-length merely rotates the digits, the block is cyclic; this rotation is the defining test.
